axes.label: Weight
axes.desc: Where the body's weight lives: pulled up and away from the floor, or yielded into it.
axes.theory: Every technique takes a stance on gravity. Classical ballet and the techniques that borrow its legs train a 'pull-up': the centre of mass held high, knees straight, the dancer appearing to rise away from the floor. Grounded techniques do the opposite. The knees soften, the pelvis drops, and the dancer learns to yield weight into the floor so they can push off it. Irmgard Bartenieff called this 'yield and push': you can only push away from a surface you have first given weight to. Many African-diasporic forms, Butoh's bent-legged ganimata stance and most release-based work sit at the grounded end. The axis is not about strength. A grounded dancer can be very light on their feet, but the reference point is down, not up.

rubric.0: Centre of mass held high; straight standing legs; relevé and balances are the norm.
rubric.0.5: Neutral stance; pliés used as preparation rather than as a home position.
rubric.1: Knees habitually bent, pelvis low, weight visibly poured into the feet and floor.

axes.watch: Watch the knees and the height of the pelvis between movements. Do they return to straight, or stay soft?

axes.label: Torso
axes.desc: How much the spine bends, contracts and twists instead of staying a vertical column.
axes.theory: Ballet keeps the torso largely vertical and quiet so the legs and arms can be read clearly. Modern dance began by setting the spine free. Martha Graham made the torso the source of expression. Her contraction hollows the body from the pelvis on an exhale, and her spiral rotates the torso around the vertical axis. Merce Cunningham taught five positions of the back: upright, curve, arch, tilt and twist. Horton favours long flat backs and lateral tilts, which are articulate but planar rather than curved. Gaga and Dunham work with fluid, undulating or isolating spines. A high score means the spine itself is a main moving part, bending in several directions, not just a support for the limbs.

rubric.0: Spine kept vertical and still; expression comes from the limbs.
rubric.0.5: Spine tilts or flat-backs in clear planes, but curves and twists are occasional.
rubric.1: Contraction, arch, spiral and undulation are central to the vocabulary.

axes.watch: Follow the line from the tailbone to the head. Does it stay straight, or does it curve and twist?

axes.label: Dynamics
axes.desc: The energy shape of a phrase: smooth and continuous, or sharp attacks and stops.
axes.theory: Rudolf Laban described the quality of movement through four Effort factors. Two matter most here: Time (sudden versus sustained) and Flow (bound versus free). A sustained phrase spreads its energy evenly, so motion never quite stops. A percussive phrase concentrates energy into accents: a quick attack, then a held shape or a rebound. Graham's contractions are strikes from the pelvis. Dunham's isolations play several rhythms against one another (polyrhythm). Butoh can slow movement almost to stillness. Doris Humphrey's 'suspension', the moment a body hangs at the top of an arc before falling, sits between the two: a held breath inside a continuous flow. In the animated figure, this axis sets transition speed and how long each step holds.

rubric.0: Continuous, slow, unaccented flow; stillness and slowness are valued.
rubric.0.5: A mix of accents and flow; phrasing follows breath or music.
rubric.1: Sharp attacks, stops, rhythmic accents and fast changes dominate.

axes.watch: Look at how a movement starts and ends. Does it melt in and out, or click into place?

axes.label: Floor
axes.desc: How much of the technique happens on, into and through the floor.
axes.theory: Ballet treats the floor as a surface to push away from. Early modern dance brought dancers down to it. Graham's class begins seated on the floor with bounces, breathings and spirals, and Horton and Limón teach falls to the ground. But in those techniques the floor is mostly a place to practise or a destination. In later forms it becomes a partner. Release classes often start lying in constructive rest, using the floor to release tension. Contact Improvisation rolls across it continuously. David Zambrano's Flying Low is designed for travelling at speed in and out of the floor, with spirals that pass the body through low levels without stopping. A high score means time spent near the ground and smooth passage between levels, not just going down and getting up.

rubric.0: Almost everything happens standing; going to the floor is rare.
rubric.0.5: Floor work as a warm-up section or in set falls.
rubric.1: Continuous travel through low levels; the floor is part of nearly every phrase.

axes.watch: Count how much time the dancer spends below standing height, and how smoothly they pass through it.

axes.label: Initiation
axes.desc: Where movement starts: hands, feet and points in space, or the pelvis, breath and centre.
axes.theory: Any movement starts somewhere. In centre-initiated techniques the impulse begins in the pelvis, the belly or the breath and travels outward through the spine to the limbs, as a ripple (sequential or 'successional' movement). Graham's contraction starts in the pelvis, Limón phrases begin on the breath, and Flying Low organises spirals around the centre. In periphery-initiated work, the hands, feet or head lead and the rest of the body follows. William Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies are the clearest case: the dancer imagines points, lines and planes in Laban's kinesphere (the sphere of space within reach) and moves the limbs to draw, touch or extrude them. Bartenieff's core–distal connectivity describes the link between the two: in an integrated mover, energy passes both ways between centre and extremities.

rubric.0: Limbs lead; spatial targets (points, lines) organise the movement.
rubric.0.5: Both are used; initiation depends on the exercise.
rubric.1: Movement is consistently driven from the pelvis, breath or centre.

axes.watch: Watch the first quarter-second of a movement: which body part moves before the others?

axes.label: Structure
axes.desc: A fixed vocabulary taught as set exercises, or tasks and principles you improvise from.
axes.theory: Codified techniques are passed on as a syllabus: named exercises in a fixed order, practised daily until the vocabulary becomes second nature. Graham, Horton, Limón, Dunham and Cunningham classes look recognisably similar anywhere in the world. From the 1960s the Judson Dance Theater group in New York challenged this, building dances from tasks, rules and everyday movement. Their descendants teach principles instead of steps. Contact Improvisation has no set vocabulary at all, only physical skills and a shared attention. Gaga is taught entirely through spoken images, without mirrors. Forsythe's technologies are rules for generating movement. Countertechnique sits in the middle: a structured class whose aim is to give dancers tools rather than fixed shapes. The scale says nothing about rigour: improvised forms train skills as demanding as any syllabus.

rubric.0: No fixed vocabulary; tasks, images or scores generate the movement each time.
rubric.0.5: A structured class built around principles; exercises vary.
rubric.1: Named, fixed exercises in a set order, the same from class to class.

axes.watch: Ask whether two classes on different days would contain the same exercises.

axes.label: Balance
axes.desc: Whether balance is something to keep, or something to give up and catch again.
axes.theory: Doris Humphrey described dance as 'the arc between two deaths': standing in perfect balance and lying motionless on the floor. Life, and dance, happen in between, in the risk of falling and recovering. Her student José Limón built a technique around falling, rebounding and suspending. Cunningham and ballet value secure, held balance, even in fast changes of direction. Contact Improvisation trains falling as a basic skill. Countertechnique sends body parts in opposite directions so dancers can go far off balance without strain. A high score means the technique deliberately leaves the vertical and treats the recovery as part of the movement, not a correction.

rubric.0: Balance is held and controlled; going off-axis is avoided or brief.
rubric.0.5: Off-balance tilts and falls appear as specific exercises.
rubric.1: Falling, catching and rebounding run through the whole vocabulary.

axes.watch: Does the body ever lean past the point where it would have to step or fall to recover?

axes.label: Contact
axes.desc: How much the practice depends on touching, leaning on and carrying another body.
axes.theory: Most dance techniques are trained solo, facing a mirror or the front of the room. Partnering, if taught, is a separate skill: ballet's pas de deux puts it in a different class. Contact Improvisation reversed this in 1972. Its basic unit is two bodies sharing a moving point of contact, giving and taking weight, rolling over and lifting one another without fixed roles. Release work and Flying Low often include group and partner exercises, but these extend solo training rather than define it. This axis measures how essential another body is to the practice.

rubric.0: Trained alone; partnering is absent or a separate discipline.
rubric.0.5: Regular partner or group work inside class.
rubric.1: The practice cannot exist without shared weight and touch.

axes.watch: Could you practise this technique alone in a room? How much would be lost?

techniques.name: Wigman (Ausdruckstanz)
techniques.summary: German expressionist dance: movement driven by inner feeling, tension and release, and the dancer's struggle with space.
techniques.history: Mary Wigman studied rhythmic gymnastics with Émile Jaques-Dalcroze and then worked with Rudolf Laban at Monte Verità in Switzerland during the First World War. In 1920 she opened her school in Dresden, which became the centre of Ausdruckstanz ('expressive dance'). Her dances, often performed to percussion or in silence and sometimes in masks, treated space as a living force the dancer pushes against. Her student Hanya Holm brought her teaching to New York in 1931, where it fed into American modern dance through Alwin Nikolais and others.
principles: Space as a partner to struggle with
Dance independent of music: percussion or silence

concepts.desc: 'Expressive dance': the German modern dance movement of the 1910s–30s that put inner experience before set form.
Wigman's basic polarity: the body gathering energy into extreme tension, then letting it go.
Not an empty container but a force: the dancer reaches into it, pushes against it and is pushed back.
Long turning sequences that carry the dancer into a trance-like state.

exercises: Improvised studies on a theme, often with percussion
techniques.legacy: Through Hanya Holm and Alwin Nikolais it shaped American modern dance; through Kazuo Ohno's teachers it reached Butoh.
techniques.distinct: Wigman combines a strongly curved, expressive torso with a centre-driven impulse, like Graham, but teaches through improvised studies rather than a fixed syllabus. In the space its nearest neighbours are Gaga and Taylor; its signature is the swing between extreme tension and release, and the dancer's struggle with space.

notes.grounding: A low, strong stance; weight is used to press into space and the floor.
notes.torso: The torso bends, contracts and twists to carry emotion.
notes.dynamics: Sharp swings between extreme tension and sudden release.
notes.floor: Kneeling, crouching and seated dances (like the Witch Dance) are central.
notes.initiation: Movement surges from the centre outward.
notes.structure: Themes and improvised studies rather than a fixed exercise order.
notes.fall: Collapses and releases are part of the tension–relaxation cycle.
notes.contact: Solo and group, but rarely shared weight.

techniques.why: Expressive, grounded, centre-driven work organised around tension and release, taught through themed improvisations.

people.name: Mary Wigman
people.path: Trained in Dalcroze eurhythmics at Hellerau, then with Rudolf Laban at Monte Verità (Ascona) from 1913.
people.story: Wigman began dancing late, in her mid-twenties, and found her voice with Laban during the First World War. Her solo Hexentanz (Witch Dance), danced seated and masked, became the emblem of German expressionist dance. Her Dresden school drew students from across Europe and America. Her career was disrupted under the Nazi regime and the war; afterwards she taught in Leipzig and then West Berlin, where she staged Le Sacre du printemps in 1957.
people.belief: Dance should come from inner experience, and space is a living force the dancer must struggle with.

class.name: Tension and relaxation
class.desc: The class gathers energy into the whole body and releases it, again and again.
class.notice: Fists, raised shoulders and a curled spine at full tension; everything drops on release.

class.name: Reaching into space
class.desc: Big diagonal reaches and swings that push against the surrounding space.
class.notice: The reach comes from the centre and travels out to the fingertips.

class.name: Turning
class.desc: Long turns on the spot, often with rising arms, building towards ecstasy.
class.notice: The head and chest lift as the turn speeds up.

class.name: Expressive study
class.desc: An improvised study on a theme: here, the seated, clawing Witch Dance.
class.notice: Clawed hands, raised shoulders and the weight sunk into the floor.

techniques.name: Graham
techniques.summary: The first codified modern dance technique: dramatic, percussive and built on the contraction and release of the torso.
techniques.history: Martha Graham trained and performed with Denishawn, Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn's company, before leaving in 1923 to find a movement language of her own. She founded her school and company in New York in 1926 and developed the technique through the 1930s, working closely with her mentor, the composer Louis Horst. She wanted movement that showed inner, emotional life rather than decoration. Her vocabulary of contraction, spiral and fall became the first widely taught alternative to ballet, and generations of modern dancers trained in it, including Merce Cunningham, Paul Taylor and Ohad Naharin.
principles: Spiral of the torso around the spine
Floor work as the opening of class
Breath as the motor of movement

concepts.desc: An exhale that hollows the torso from the pelvis upward, curving the spine. Percussive and emotionally charged.
The inhale that returns the spine to length and verticality, often lifting the chest.
Rotation of the torso around the spine, starting from the pelvis, with the back carried higher than the front.
Exercises of contraction and release on the knees with the arms reaching.

exercises: Bounces, breathings and spirals seated on the floor
Pleadings and exercises on the knees
Triplets and progressions across the floor
techniques.legacy: Still taught worldwide; it set the template for later codified modern techniques.
techniques.distinct: Graham combines the strongest torso articulation in the set with a strictly codified class and percussive dynamics. The spine does the expressive work, but always inside fixed forms. Dunham is close on rhythm and grounding; Release shares the curved spine but not the structure.

notes.grounding: Strong use of plié and the floor, but standing work still lifts through the back.
notes.torso: The contraction and spiral make the spine the main expressive instrument.
notes.dynamics: Contractions are sharp strikes from the pelvis; phrasing is dramatic and accented.
notes.floor: Class opens seated on the floor, and set falls are central, but most dancing is upright.
notes.initiation: Nearly every movement starts in the pelvis and breath.
notes.structure: A fixed syllabus taught in a set order.
notes.fall: Graham falls are trained, but as controlled descents rather than off-balance risk.
notes.contact: A solo training; partnering appears only in repertoire.

techniques.why: The contraction is a sharp, pelvis-driven curve of the spine, practised as a fixed class order that starts seated on the floor.

people.name: Martha Graham
people.path: Saw Ruth St. Denis perform in 1911 and trained at Denishawn in Los Angeles from 1916.
people.story: Graham left Denishawn in 1923 and founded her school and company in New York in 1926. Working with the composer Louis Horst, she stripped away decoration to find movement that showed inner, emotional life. She danced until 1969 and made more than 180 works, many on Greek myth and American themes. Her collaborators included Isamu Noguchi (sets) and Aaron Copland (Appalachian Spring).
people.belief: Movement never lies: the body reveals inner truth, and the contraction is the shape of that feeling.

class.name: Floor: bounces and breathings
class.desc: Seated with soles together, the class bounces forward and then breathes in contractions and releases.
class.notice: The contraction starts in the pelvis on the exhale; the release lifts the back on the inhale.

class.name: Floor: spirals and pleadings
class.desc: Spirals sitting in fourth position, then exercises on the knees.
class.notice: The spiral turns around the spine, with the back held higher than the front.

class.name: Standing centre
class.desc: Contractions, releases and spirals standing, with pliés.
class.notice: The same torso work as on the floor, now on two feet.

class.name: Falls
class.desc: Controlled descents to the floor and recoveries.
class.notice: The fall is shaped and timed, never an accident.

class.name: Across the floor: triplets
class.desc: Travelling triplets (down–up–up) and walks.
class.notice: The rhythm: a bent-knee step, then two on half-toe.

techniques.name: Humphrey–Weidman
techniques.summary: The theory of fall and recovery: dance as the arc between balance and collapse, phrased by the breath.
techniques.history: Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman both danced with Denishawn. They left in 1928 to form their own company and school in New York. Humphrey built a theory of movement around 'fall and recovery': the body giving in to gravity and then recovering from it, with the most exciting moments in between. Weidman added humour, pantomime and character dances. Humphrey later stopped performing through arthritis and became artistic director of José Limón's company. Her book The Art of Making Dances (1959) became a standard text on choreography.

concepts.desc: Yielding to gravity and recovering from it: the basic rhythm of all movement for Humphrey.
Perfect balance and complete collapse are both stillness; dance lives between them.
Phrases built on the rise and fall of breathing rather than counted metre.
Weidman's stylised, often comic gesture, taking everyday action into dance.

exercises: Breath rhythm: rising on the inhale, falling on the exhale
Side and forward falls with recovery
Successional waves through the spine and arms
Group studies in unison and opposition
techniques.legacy: Its principles continue directly in the Limón technique.
techniques.distinct: Humphrey–Weidman sits right next to Limón, its direct descendant, with the second-highest fall score in the set. It is slightly less grounded and codified than Limón, and it carries Weidman's pantomime as well as Humphrey's architecture.

notes.grounding: Weight is given to gravity and recovered from it.
notes.torso: Successional movement passes through a mobile spine.
notes.dynamics: Breath rhythm: rising, suspending and falling rather than striking.
notes.floor: Falls reach the floor, but most dancing is upright.
notes.initiation: Breath and the shift of weight start the movement.
notes.structure: A clear class and choreographic method, though less fixed than Graham's.
notes.fall: The heart of the theory: fall and recovery.
notes.contact: Group work and some partnering in the choreography.

techniques.why: Fall and recovery on the breath, taught through a structured but flexible class.

people.name: Doris Humphrey
people.path: Taught dance in Chicago, then joined Denishawn in 1917.
people.story: Humphrey left Denishawn with Charles Weidman in 1928. She built her theory of fall and recovery and made group works of architectural clarity such as Water Study and The Shakers. Arthritis ended her performing career in the mid-1940s; she then directed José Limón's company and taught composition at Juilliard. Her book The Art of Making Dances was published after her death.
people.belief: All movement lies on an arc between two deaths: perfect balance and complete collapse.

people.name: Charles Weidman
people.path: Trained at Denishawn after seeing Ruth St. Denis perform.
people.story: Weidman co-directed the Humphrey–Weidman company and brought wit, satire and stylised pantomime to modern dance, from comic character pieces to the anti-lynching drama Lynchtown.
people.belief: Everyday gesture, exaggerated and shaped, can carry both comedy and tragedy.

class.name: Breath rhythm
class.desc: Rising on the inhale, falling on the exhale.
class.notice: No counts: the phrase follows the breath.

class.name: Fall and recovery
class.desc: Swings, side falls and recoveries, with suspension at the top.
class.notice: The moment of suspension before the body gives in to gravity.

class.name: Water Study
class.desc: Humphrey's wave-like study: kneeling bodies curl and rise like water.
class.notice: Successive waves pass through the spine from the pelvis.

class.name: Weidman pantomime
class.desc: Expressive gesture and character, taken from Weidman's teaching.
class.notice: Gestures are exaggerated and shaped, not mimed realistically.

techniques.name: Horton
techniques.summary: An anatomically based technique of long lines, flat backs and lateral stretches, known for building strength and flexibility.
techniques.history: Lester Horton developed his technique in Los Angeles in the 1930s and 1940s, outside the New York modern dance scene. He drew on his interest in Native American dance, as well as Japanese and other theatre forms, and he ran one of the first racially integrated dance companies in the United States. His students included Alvin Ailey, Carmen de Lavallade and James Truitte. After Horton's death in 1953 his students preserved and codified the technique. It is still a core of training at the Ailey School.
principles: Long lines through the whole body
Studies that build strength and flexibility

concepts.desc: Exercises designed to strengthen specific parts of the body, numbered and practised in sequence.
The body tilted sideways from the hip, with the torso and one leg forming a straight horizontal line.
Leaning back in a straight line from the knees, with the body as a single plank.
Longer set combinations, such as dimensional tonus, that put the fortifications together.

techniques.legacy: The basis of training at the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater.
techniques.distinct: Horton is codified like Graham, but its torso works in straight planes rather than curves: flat back, lateral T, hinge. It is the most geometric of the codified modern techniques, which places it near Cunningham and Countertechnique in the space.

notes.grounding: Deep lunges and squats sit alongside long, lifted lines; neither dominates.
notes.torso: Very articulate, but mostly in straight planes (flat back, tilt) rather than curves.
notes.dynamics: Controlled and even, with accents built into the studies.
notes.floor: Some floor work, but most exercises are standing.
notes.initiation: Line and shape matter as much as the centre; the whole limb moves as one.
notes.structure: Numbered fortifications and studies form a strict syllabus.
notes.fall: Hinges and tilts go off the vertical under control rather than as true falls.

techniques.why: A strongly codified anatomical system; the torso works in straight planes (flat back, lateral T) more than curves.

people.name: Lester Horton
people.path: Studied Native American dance and ballet; moved to Los Angeles in the late 1920s.
people.story: Working outside New York, Horton built a technique designed to correct anatomical weaknesses and prepare dancers for anything. His Lester Horton Dance Theater, with its own theatre in Hollywood, was one of the first racially integrated dance companies in the US. He died of a heart attack at 47; his students preserved and codified the technique.
people.belief: A dancer's body should be trained without stylistic limits, ready for any choreography.

class.name: Flat backs and laterals
class.desc: Flat backs forward and lateral stretches to the side.
class.notice: The back stays straight as a table from tailbone to head.

class.name: Fortifications
class.desc: Strength studies: hinges and deep lunges.
class.notice: In the hinge, knee to head forms one straight line.

class.name: Balances
class.desc: The lateral T and the coccyx balance.
class.notice: In the lateral T, torso and lifted leg form a single horizontal line.

class.name: Primitive squat
class.desc: The deep, flat-footed squat from Horton's study of Native American dance.
class.notice: Heels stay down; the spine stays long.

class.name: Progressions
class.desc: Lunge progressions across the floor with T arms.
class.notice: Long lines from fingertip to fingertip.

techniques.name: Dunham
techniques.summary: A synthesis of Afro-Caribbean dance, ballet and modern dance, built on isolations and polyrhythm.
techniques.history: Katherine Dunham trained as an anthropologist at the University of Chicago and did fieldwork on dance in Haiti, Jamaica, Martinique and Trinidad in 1935–36. She brought what she learned into her choreography and teaching, combining African-diasporic movement with ballet and modern dance. Her Dunham School of Dance and Theatre opened in New York in 1945 and trained dancers, actors and musicians. She saw dance as part of culture and community, not only as stage art.
principles: Isolations of the hips, ribs and shoulders
Grounded stance and rhythmic connection to drums

concepts.desc: Moving one part of the body (head, shoulders, ribs, hips) independently of the others.
Different body parts keeping different rhythms at once, as in many West African and Caribbean dances.
Set combinations travelling across the floor, building in complexity.
Dunham's idea that movement makes sense in the context of its cultural purpose.

exercises: Barre work combining ballet and isolations
Isolations of head, shoulders, ribs and pelvis
Rhythmic walks and turns to live drumming
techniques.legacy: A major influence on jazz dance, African-American concert dance and dance anthropology.
techniques.distinct: Dunham is grounded, centre-driven and percussive like Graham, which is why they sit close together. The difference lies in rhythm and isolation: the hips, ribs and shoulders move independently in layered rhythms, where Graham moves the torso as one unit.

notes.grounding: A low, bent-kneed stance connected to the earth and the drum.
notes.torso: Isolations and undulations make the torso highly articulate.
notes.dynamics: Rhythmic and accented, often with polyrhythm.
notes.initiation: Pelvis and ribs drive much of the movement.
notes.structure: A set barre and progressions, taught as a system.
notes.fall: Balance is mostly held; the emphasis is rhythm, not falling.
notes.contact: Solo and ensemble rather than partnered weight-sharing.

techniques.why: Grounded, pelvis-centred and rhythmic, with an articulate, isolating torso taught through set progressions.

people.name: Katherine Dunham
people.path: Studied anthropology at the University of Chicago alongside ballet and modern dance.
people.story: A fellowship took Dunham to Jamaica, Martinique, Trinidad and Haiti in 1935–36 to study dance. She turned that research into stage works and a technique, and her company toured more than 50 countries. She founded her New York school in 1945 and later a cultural centre in East St. Louis. In 1992, aged 82, she went on a 47-day hunger strike to protest US policy towards Haitian refugees.
people.belief: Dance carries a culture's knowledge; form and function belong together.

class.name: Barre
class.desc: Ballet-based barre: pliés and tendus.
class.notice: Ballet placement in the legs, released energy in the torso.

class.name: Isolations
class.desc: Head, shoulders, ribs and hips moved one at a time.
class.notice: Only one part moves; everything else stays still.

class.name: Progressions
class.desc: Dunham walks and travelling combinations to live drums.
class.notice: The pelvis and ribs keep different rhythms while travelling.

techniques.name: Limón
techniques.summary: A technique of weight, breath and gravity: falling, rebounding and suspending.
techniques.history: Doris Humphrey left Denishawn with Charles Weidman in 1928 and developed a theory of movement built on fall and recovery. José Limón, born in Mexico, danced with Humphrey–Weidman and then founded his own company in 1946 with Humphrey as artistic director. The Limón technique grew from Humphrey's principles and Limón's own humanist, dramatic choreography. It focuses on the natural rhythm of breath, the weight of body parts, and the moment of suspension before a fall.

concepts.desc: Giving in to gravity and recovering from it; Humphrey's core idea.
The moment of hang at the top of an arc, before gravity takes over again.
The elastic recovery that comes out of a fall, using momentum rather than muscle alone.
Feeling and using the actual weight of the head, arms and torso as they drop and swing.

exercises: Swings of the torso and arms
Head and torso drops with rebound
Falls to the floor and recovery
techniques.legacy: Its focus on weight and breath prepared the ground for release-based work.
techniques.distinct: Limón has the highest fall score in the set. It is codified and breath-driven like Graham, but its subject is gravity rather than the torso's emotional shape. Its nearest neighbour, at 96%, is Humphrey–Weidman, the source it grew from, followed by Taylor and Countertechnique.

notes.grounding: Weight is felt and given into the floor; the dancer works with gravity, not against it.
notes.torso: The spine drops, swings and curves successionally.
notes.dynamics: Phrasing follows the breath, alternating suspension and release.
notes.floor: Falls to the floor are trained, and recovery from the ground is part of the vocabulary.
notes.initiation: Breath and the drop of weight start most movement.
notes.structure: A recognisable class structure, but less rigid than Graham or Horton.
notes.fall: The core of the technique: fall, rebound, suspension.
notes.contact: Mostly solo, with some partnering in repertoire.

techniques.why: Built on Humphrey's 'arc between two deaths': giving in to gravity and suspending out of it, on the breath.

people.name: José Limón
people.path: Moved to the US as a child and studied painting in New York before seeing Harald Kreutzberg dance in 1928.
people.story: Limón joined the Humphrey–Weidman company, served in the army in the Second World War, and founded his own company in 1946 with Doris Humphrey as artistic director. His dances, including The Moor's Pavane, were dramatic and humanist, and he was a founding member of Juilliard's dance faculty.
people.belief: Dance should express the dignity and struggle of human beings, using weight, breath and gravity.

class.name: Swings
class.desc: Arm and torso swings using weight and momentum.
class.notice: The drop, the rebound, and the moment of suspension at the top.

class.name: Drops and succession
class.desc: Head and torso drops, and successional movement of the arms.
class.notice: Weight is felt: the head is heavy as it drops.

class.name: Fall and rebound
class.desc: Falls to the side and the rebound out of them.
class.notice: The fall is used to gather energy for the recovery.

class.name: Across the floor
class.desc: Runs with suspension and phrases built on breath.
class.notice: The lift at the top of each run.

techniques.name: Hawkins
techniques.summary: A technique of effortless, free-flowing movement, informed by anatomy and Eastern aesthetics, starting from the pelvis.
techniques.history: Erick Hawkins studied Greek at Harvard before training in dance. In 1938 he became the first man to dance in Martha Graham's company, and he was married to Graham from 1948 to 1954. Leaving her company, he rejected what he saw as strain and forced tension in modern dance. Drawing on kinesiology, the ideas of Lulu Sweigard and Mabel Todd, and Zen and Asian art, he developed a technique of 'free flow' and effortlessness. He worked for decades with the composer Lucia Dlugoszewski.
principles: Free flow instead of forced tension

concepts.desc: Letting movement travel through the body without blocking it with excess muscle.
Doing only the work needed, using gravity and momentum.
The pelvis is the source and controller of movement.
Being fully aware of sensation while moving, rather than imposing a shape.

exercises: Floor work on pelvic and spinal mobility
Free-flow swings of arms and legs
techniques.legacy: An early American precursor of release and somatic approaches.
techniques.distinct: Hawkins comes from Graham but removes her tension: the result is centre-driven like Graham, yet one of the most sustained, least percussive techniques in the set, with the quietest torso of all. Its nearest neighbour, at 88%, is Klein.

notes.grounding: Easy, released weight, neither pulled up nor sunk.
notes.torso: The spine moves freely but without dramatic curves.
notes.floor: Floor work opens class; most dancing is standing.
notes.fall: Balance is soft rather than risked.

techniques.why: Graham-trained but tension-free: effortless, pelvis-led free flow in a structured class.

people.name: Erick Hawkins
people.path: Studied Greek at Harvard, trained at the School of American Ballet, then joined Martha Graham's company in 1938.
people.story: Hawkins was the first man in Graham's company and her husband from 1948 to 1954. After they separated he founded his own company and developed a technique of effortless free flow, influenced by kinesiology and Asian aesthetics. Many of his dances were made with the composer Lucia Dlugoszewski.
people.belief: Movement should be effortless and natural; strain and violence have no place in dance.

class.name: Floor work
class.desc: Lying and seated work on the pelvis and spine.
class.notice: Minimal effort: the floor does the supporting.

class.name: Free-flow swings
class.desc: Arm and leg swings that let movement flow without blocking.
class.notice: Nothing is held; each swing passes into the next.

class.name: Walking from the pelvis
class.desc: Walks led by the pelvis.
class.notice: The pelvis arrives before the feet.

class.name: Arcs and balances
class.desc: Arcs traced by the arms and soft balances.
class.notice: Balance without gripping.

techniques.name: Cunningham
techniques.summary: A fast, precise technique combining ballet legs with a highly mobile back, designed for constant changes of direction.
techniques.history: Merce Cunningham danced as a soloist in Martha Graham's company from 1939 to 1945, then broke away to make work free of narrative and emotional drama. He formed his company in 1953 at Black Mountain College and collaborated for decades with the composer John Cage. They used chance procedures to decide the order and timing of movement, and made music and dance independently. His technique had to prepare dancers for anything: sudden changes of direction, speed and complex coordination of legs and back.
principles: Curve, arch, tilt and twist of the upper back
Rhythmic precision without depending on the music

concepts.desc: Upright, curve, arch, tilt and twist: the back's vocabulary, combined with the legs.
Using dice, coins or the I Ching to decide sequence, timing or space. This is a choreographic method, not part of the class.
Music and dance share a time frame but are made separately.
No single front; every point on stage can matter equally.

exercises: Bounces and back exercises in the centre
Tendu, dégagé and leg work at speed
Fast across-the-floor phrases with changes of direction
techniques.legacy: Influenced postmodern dance via his students and Judson, and made chance a choreographic tool.
techniques.distinct: Cunningham is the most upright technique here, joint most lifted with Forsythe, and has the most securely held balance. Its back is very mobile but organised in clear named shapes, and its legs come from ballet. It sits near Horton, Nikolais and Forsythe: geometric, upright, and led from the limbs as much as from the centre.

notes.grounding: Ballet pull-up in the legs; weight carried high for speed.
notes.torso: The upper back curves, arches, tilts and twists, but in clear, named positions.
notes.dynamics: Quick, precise and often unpredictable in rhythm.
notes.initiation: Legs and back are coordinated as separate parts; little sense of a pelvic source.
notes.structure: A set class; chance belongs to choreography, not training.
notes.fall: Balance is controlled and held, even in fast direction changes.

techniques.why: Upright and quick on ballet legs; the back bends in five set directions while balance stays sharply controlled.

people.name: Merce Cunningham
people.path: Studied at the Cornish School in Seattle, where he met John Cage; danced as a soloist with Martha Graham, 1939–45.
people.story: Cunningham founded his company in 1953 at Black Mountain College. With Cage he separated dance from music and used chance procedures to make choreographic decisions. He collaborated with artists like Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns, and in later life used computer software to make dances. He choreographed until his death at 90.
people.belief: Dance is about movement itself; any point in space and any moment can matter equally.

class.name: Back exercises
class.desc: Upright, curve, arch, tilt and twist, combined with the legs.
class.notice: The legs stay in ballet positions while the back changes shape.

class.name: Legs at speed
class.desc: Tendus and dégagés at different speeds and directions.
class.notice: Speed comes from precise, light feet.

class.name: Adagio and balance
class.desc: Slow extensions and long balances.
class.notice: Long balances held without effort.

class.name: Across the floor
class.desc: Fast phrases with jumps and sudden changes of direction.
class.notice: The body changes front without warning.

techniques.name: Nikolais / Louis
techniques.summary: Movement as motion, not emotion: decentralised initiation from any body part, and the study of space, time, shape and motion.
techniques.history: Alwin Nikolais trained with Hanya Holm, Mary Wigman's student, and began teaching at the Henry Street Playhouse in New York in 1948. With his partner Murray Louis he developed a teaching method built on improvisation and the elements of space, time, shape and motion. Nikolais created a 'total theatre' of light, sound, props and costume that transformed dancers' bodies. Louis, a dancer of great wit and precision, refined the technique and led his own company.
principles: Space, time, shape and motion as material

concepts.desc: The centre of movement can be anywhere: an elbow, a knee, the top of the head.
The dancer's subject is movement itself, not personal feeling.
The four elements studied and improvised on in class.
Light, sound, props and costume as equal partners with the dancer.

exercises: Isolations led by single body parts
techniques.legacy: Influenced multimedia dance and the teaching of improvisation and composition.
techniques.distinct: Nikolais/Louis is among the most periphery-led techniques after Forsythe: movement may start from any part. It is close to Forsythe and Gaga in the space: improvised, upright, and analytical about space.

notes.torso: Articulate, sculptural use of the torso.
notes.dynamics: Varied, with an interest in timing and rhythm.
notes.initiation: Decentralised: limbs and body parts lead.
notes.fall: Off-centre shapes appear but falling isn't the focus.
notes.contact: Group and ensemble work with some contact.

techniques.why: Decentralised, improvisational study of space, time, shape and motion.

people.name: Alwin Nikolais
people.path: Worked as a silent-film accompanist and puppeteer, then studied dance with Hanya Holm.
people.story: Nikolais directed the Henry Street Playhouse in New York from 1948. He designed his own lighting, sound scores and costumes, creating abstract 'total theatre' in which dancers became moving shapes. His teaching method spread widely and he later founded a centre in France.
people.belief: Motion, not emotion: the dancer's subject is movement in space and time.

people.name: Murray Louis
people.path: Studied with Alwin Nikolais from 1949.
people.story: Louis was Nikolais's partner and leading dancer, known for his wit and precision. He developed the technique with Nikolais and ran his own company, touring widely.
people.belief: Technique should make the dancer intelligent in motion, able to move from any part of the body.

class.name: Decentralisation
class.desc: Isolations led by single body parts: an elbow, a knee.
class.notice: Watch which part leads; the rest follows.

class.name: Space and volume
class.desc: Improvisations that expand and shrink the body's volume.
class.notice: The body as a shape filling and emptying space.

class.name: Shape
class.desc: Sculptural, angular studies.
class.notice: Angles and planes, not feelings.

class.name: Composition
class.desc: Short assignments combining space, time, shape and motion.
class.notice: Clear choices about timing and direction.

techniques.name: Taylor
techniques.summary: Athletic, musical and weighty: Graham's torso and Cunningham's speed applied to runs, falls and lyrical phrases.
techniques.history: Paul Taylor came to dance from swimming and painting at Syracuse University. He danced with Martha Graham's company from 1955 to 1962, also worked with Merce Cunningham, and guested with George Balanchine at New York City Ballet. He founded his own company in 1954 and made about 150 dances, from the lyrical Aureole (1962) to Esplanade (1975), built from walking, running, sliding and falling. His class uses a Graham-derived warm-up but emphasises momentum, weight and space-covering movement.

concepts.desc: A strong, mobile torso, often tilting and twisting in big shapes.
Using the weight and speed of the body to carry movement through space.
Walking, running and falling raised to full-out dance (as in Esplanade).
Long, singing phrases closely tied to the music.

exercises: Tilts and back work in the centre
Runs, leaps and slides across the floor
techniques.legacy: One of the most performed American modern dance repertoires.
techniques.distinct: Taylor sits close to the Humphrey–Limón line and to Countertechnique: an expressive torso inherited from Graham, a love of falling and momentum, and more partnering than any technique except Contact.

notes.grounding: Weighty and grounded in runs and falls, lifted in lyrical passages.
notes.torso: The 'Taylor back': big tilts and twists.
notes.floor: Falls and slides reach the floor.
notes.initiation: Weight shifts through the centre drive the movement.
notes.structure: A set warm-up and a recognisable class.
notes.fall: Falls and slides at speed are part of the vocabulary.
notes.contact: Plenty of partnering and lifts in the repertoire.

techniques.why: Graham's torso with momentum, falls and partnering, taught through a set class.

people.name: Paul Taylor
people.path: Swam and painted at Syracuse University before training at Juilliard and with Graham.
people.story: Taylor danced with Martha Graham from 1955 to 1962 and with Merce Cunningham, and guested with George Balanchine. He founded his company in 1954. His early experiments included standing still on stage; he went on to make about 150 works ranging from joyful to dark, including Aureole and Esplanade.
people.belief: Ordinary movement like walking, running and falling can become extraordinary dance.

class.name: Warm-up
class.desc: A Graham-derived warm-up on the floor.
class.notice: The contraction, but used for momentum rather than drama.

class.name: Centre: tilts and back
class.desc: Big Taylor tilts and lyrical arms.
class.notice: The whole body tilts as one line.

class.name: Runs, leaps and falls
class.desc: Running, leaping and falling across the space.
class.notice: Momentum carries the body; the fall is part of the run.

techniques.name: Butoh
techniques.summary: A Japanese avant-garde dance form of extreme slowness and transformation, driven by images rather than steps.
techniques.history: Butoh emerged in post-war Japan. Tatsumi Hijikata's Kinjiki (Forbidden Colours, 1959) is often named as its starting point, and Hijikata called his work ankoku butoh, 'dance of darkness'. Kazuo Ohno, who had studied with teachers trained in German Ausdruckstanz, became its other founding figure. His Admiring La Argentina (1977) is a landmark. Butoh rejected both Western dance and Japanese classical forms and looked for the body's hidden, raw and transformed states. Companies such as Sankai Juku later took it worldwide, often with shaved heads and white body paint.
principles: The body being moved rather than moving
Facing darkness, death and the grotesque

concepts.desc: 'Dance of darkness': Hijikata's name for the form, rejecting beauty and virtuosity.
Hijikata's notation of images (for example, insects crawling on the skin) that the dancer embodies.
A low, bow-legged stance with the knees bent and turned out, the weight sunk.
Letting images or forces move the body instead of willing a movement.

exercises: Very slow walking (for example, as if on a thin line)
Image work: transforming into an animal, plant or object
techniques.legacy: Spread internationally from the 1980s and influenced physical theatre and contemporary dance.
techniques.distinct: Butoh is the most sustained technique in the set and among the most grounded. Its nearest neighbours are Klein and Release: all three are low, slow and inward. It differs in purpose: Klein and Release seek ease and support, while Butoh seeks transformation and strangeness.

notes.grounding: The low, sunk ganimata stance keeps weight deep in the legs.
notes.torso: The spine distorts, curves and collapses as images transform it.
notes.dynamics: Extreme slowness; the most sustained form here.
notes.floor: Crawling, lying and low levels are common, alongside standing work.
notes.initiation: Movement comes from inner images and the centre rather than from the limbs.
notes.structure: Images and states rather than a step syllabus.
notes.fall: Collapses and descents occur, but slowly and under control.

techniques.why: Deeply grounded and almost continuously slow; worked through images rather than a fixed step vocabulary.

people.name: Tatsumi Hijikata
people.path: Studied German-influenced modern dance and jazz dance in Japan.
people.story: Hijikata's Kinjiki (Forbidden Colours, 1959) shocked audiences and is often named as the birth of Butoh. He called his work ankoku butoh, 'dance of darkness', and developed butoh-fu, a notation of images for dancers to embody.
people.belief: The body holds hidden, rejected states; dance should bring them to light.

people.name: Kazuo Ohno
people.path: Studied with Baku Ishii and Takaya Eguchi, teachers shaped by German Ausdruckstanz.
people.story: Ohno worked closely with Hijikata, and his solo Admiring La Argentina (1977) became a landmark. He toured the world and kept performing into his nineties, his son Yoshito continuing the work.
people.belief: Dance comes from the soul and from memory; the dancer is moved rather than moving.

class.name: Ganimata stance
class.desc: Finding the low, bow-legged stance.
class.notice: Knees bent and open, weight sunk deep.

class.name: Slow walk
class.desc: Walking as slowly as possible, as if on a thin line.
class.notice: Each step takes many seconds.

class.name: Image work
class.desc: Embodying images: becoming a flower, an insect, smoke.
class.notice: The body is moved by the image, not by will.

class.name: Collapse
class.desc: Slow descent towards the floor.
class.notice: Even the collapse is controlled and slow.

techniques.name: Release Technique
techniques.founder: Joan Skinner, Mary Fulkerson and others
techniques.summary: A family of approaches that replace muscular holding with skeletal alignment, imagery and the efficient use of gravity and momentum.
techniques.history: Release is less a single technique than a family. It goes back to Mabel Todd's The Thinking Body (1937) and Lulu Sweigard's ideokinesis, which used mental images to improve alignment. In the 1960s and 1970s, teachers including Joan Skinner (Skinner Releasing Technique) in the US and Mary Fulkerson at Dartington College in the UK built dance classes on these ideas. The postmodern choreographers around Judson, Trisha Brown above all, made release-based movement the look of a generation. Today 'release' describes much of contemporary dance training in Europe and beyond.
principles: Breath and the floor as resources

concepts.desc: Using precise mental images of the skeleton and movement to change habits without forcing.
Lying on the back with knees bent, letting the floor support the body while imagining release.
Letting a swing or drop carry the body instead of starting every movement with fresh effort.
Finding support through the bones rather than tensed muscles.

exercises: Rolling and spiralling on the floor
techniques.legacy: Shaped much European contemporary training and many somatic practices.
techniques.distinct: Release is moderately grounded, curved, floor-friendly and loosely structured, and one of the most sustained techniques. Its closest neighbours are Klein and Butoh, through slowness and inward focus, then Countertechnique. Its defining number is low effort: dynamics at 0.2.

notes.grounding: Weight is released into the floor and bones rather than held up.
notes.torso: A free, mobile spine, often spiralling and curving.
notes.dynamics: Ease and momentum; effort is minimised.
notes.floor: Much of class happens lying, rolling and passing through low levels.
notes.initiation: Starts from the skeleton and centre, though imagery can lead from anywhere.
notes.structure: Principles and images rather than set steps.
notes.fall: Uses gravity and drops, going off balance easily.
notes.contact: Touch and partner work are often used as teaching tools.

techniques.why: Lets go of held tension and trusts weight and momentum; taught through images and principles more than set steps.

people.name: Joan Skinner
people.path: Danced with Martha Graham and Merce Cunningham, then studied the Alexander Technique.
people.story: Skinner developed Skinner Releasing Technique in the 1960s and 70s, teaching at the University of Washington in Seattle. Her classes use poetic imagery and touch to release habitual tension.
people.belief: Letting go of held tension frees the dancer's natural, multidirectional movement.

people.name: Mary Fulkerson
people.path: Studied anatomy-based release work with Barbara Clark's circle in the US.
people.story: Fulkerson taught at Dartington College of Arts in England from the 1970s, making it a centre of release-based and experimental dance in Europe.
people.belief: Imagery and anatomy can replace effort and imitation in dance training.

class.name: Constructive rest
class.desc: Lying on the back with knees bent, using imagery.
class.notice: The floor takes the weight; nothing is held.

class.name: Rolling and spine
class.desc: Rolling through the floor and rolling up through the spine.
class.notice: One vertebra at a time.

class.name: Swings
class.desc: Swings using gravity and momentum.
class.notice: Let the drop carry the body.

class.name: Spiral and reach
class.desc: Phrases spiralling up from the floor into long reaches.
class.notice: Movement passes continuously between levels.

techniques.name: Contact Improvisation
techniques.founder: Steve Paxton (with Nancy Stark Smith and others)
techniques.summary: An improvised duet form in which dancers share a moving point of contact, giving and taking weight.
techniques.history: Steve Paxton danced with Merce Cunningham and was a founding member of Judson Dance Theater. In January 1972 he made Magnesium with students at Oberlin College, a piece of falling, colliding and rolling. Later that year he and others, including Nancy Stark Smith, performed what they called Contact Improvisation in New York. The form spread quickly through 'jams': open sessions where anyone can dance. Paxton drew on aikido and his own research into reflexes and the 'small dance', the tiny balancing movements of a body standing still.
principles: Following the momentum of the duet

concepts.desc: The place where two bodies touch. It rolls across the bodies and leads the dance.
Standing still and noticing the tiny reflexive movements that keep the body upright.
An open improvisation session, the main social setting of the form.
Being able to move in any direction, including upside down, without losing orientation.

exercises: Rolling point of contact with a partner
techniques.legacy: Practised in jams worldwide; it reshaped partnering in contemporary dance.
techniques.distinct: Contact is the outlier on contact (1.0) and among the least structured. Without that one axis it would sit beside Release, its close relative. With it, it stands apart from every other technique: no other form makes another body essential.

notes.grounding: Weight flows down into the floor and into the partner.
notes.torso: The back is a large, rolling surface for contact; the spine stays responsive.
notes.dynamics: Continuous flow, following momentum, with occasional sudden falls.
notes.floor: Rolling and returning to the floor are constant.
notes.initiation: The point of contact and the centre lead, more than the hands.
notes.structure: Fully improvised; skills are trained, but no vocabulary is set.
notes.fall: Falling and being caught are basic skills.
notes.contact: The defining feature: impossible without another body.

techniques.why: An improvised duet form whose whole subject is the moving point of contact and shared weight.

people.name: Steve Paxton
people.path: A gymnast and modern dancer; danced with Merce Cunningham, 1961–64, and helped found Judson Dance Theater.
people.story: In 1972 Paxton made Magnesium with students at Oberlin College and then, with others, began Contact Improvisation. He kept researching reflexes, the 'small dance' and the senses, and released the video study Material for the Spine.
people.belief: Two bodies in contact can find a dance neither would make alone, by listening to weight and momentum.

people.name: Nancy Stark Smith
people.path: A gymnast and track athlete who took part in Paxton's early Contact performances in 1972.
people.story: Stark Smith taught Contact Improvisation worldwide for almost 50 years and co-founded Contact Quarterly, the journal that connected its international community.
people.belief: The 'underscore': dancing is a practice of attention that can be shared with anyone.

class.name: The small dance
class.desc: Standing still and noticing tiny balancing movements.
class.notice: Stillness isn't static: the body keeps adjusting.

class.name: Sharing weight
class.desc: Leaning into each other and counterbalancing.
class.notice: Each partner gives and takes weight through the point of contact.

class.name: Lifts and bases
class.desc: One partner becomes a table; the other rides over the back.
class.notice: Lifts come from momentum, not muscle.

techniques.name: Klein Technique
techniques.summary: A training of deep support at the level of the bones, connecting the pelvic floor, the hip rotators and the spine.
techniques.history: Susan Klein developed her technique in New York in the 1970s, after an injury led her to study anatomy, Bartenieff Fundamentals and the ideokinetic work of Barbara Clark. She taught that dancers should work 'at the bone level', finding support from the deepest muscles near the skeleton rather than from surface tension. The Klein School in New York trained many dancers of the downtown, release-based scene, and the work is used widely for injury prevention and rehabilitation.
principles: Connection of the pelvic floor and deep hip rotators
Alignment of sitz bones and heels
Rotation from the hip, not the knees or feet

concepts.desc: Sensing and moving from the skeleton rather than from the surface muscles.
The pelvic floor and deep rotators holding the body up from inside.
A key alignment line from the sitting bones down through the heels.
The technique grew out of rehabilitation and is still used to treat injuries.

exercises: Lying floor work for deep support
Standing alignment and pelvic floor connection
works: Taught as a practice; widely used by New York release-based dancers
techniques.legacy: Influential in release-based training and dancer rehabilitation.
techniques.distinct: Klein is closest to Hawkins, Butoh and Release: grounded, centre-driven and very sustained. Its particular focus is internal support rather than any visible style.

notes.grounding: Weight through the bones into the floor.
notes.floor: Much of the work is lying or seated.
notes.initiation: Deep pelvic and hip support initiate everything.
notes.structure: A consistent sequence of exercises, applied flexibly.

techniques.why: Internal, bone-level support work: grounded, slow and centre-driven.

people.name: Susan Klein
people.path: Trained as a modern dancer in New York; studied anatomy, Bartenieff Fundamentals and Barbara Clark's ideokinesis after an injury.
people.story: Klein founded the Klein School in New York and developed her technique for healing and training. Many dancers of the downtown, release-based scene studied with her.
people.belief: Work at the bone level: real support comes from the deepest muscles next to the skeleton.

class.name: Deep support on the floor
class.desc: Lying work connecting the pelvic floor and deep hip muscles.
class.notice: Movement too small to see from outside.

class.name: Standing alignment
class.desc: Finding the line from sitting bones to heels.
class.notice: Quiet, released standing.

class.name: Roll downs
class.desc: Rolling down and up through the spine.
class.notice: Support from the bones, not surface muscles.

class.name: Rotation
class.desc: Turning the legs out from the deep hip rotators.
class.notice: Rotation comes from the hip, never the knees or feet.

techniques.name: Improvisation Technologies
techniques.summary: A set of rules for generating movement from imagined points, lines and planes, developed from ballet geometry.
techniques.history: William Forsythe directed Ballett Frankfurt from 1984 to 2004 and took classical ballet apart from the inside. To help his dancers improvise, he developed operations on the lines and shapes of the body and the space around it, building on Rudolf Laban's idea of the kinesphere. In 1994 he recorded lectures on these operations, published in 1999 by ZKM Karlsruhe as the CD-ROM Improvisation Technologies: A Tool for the Analytical Dance Eye. It became a widely used teaching resource.
principles: Points, lines and planes in space

concepts.desc: Imagining a line between two points on the body or in space, then moving it.
Drawing a shape in space with any body part.
Pushing a line or shape out along a direction, as if stretching it into space.
Letting an imagined curve fall through the body, which follows it.

exercises: Drawing lines between points of the body
Inscribing shapes with elbows, knees, head
techniques.legacy: Changed how ballet dancers improvise and how dancers think about space and geometry.
techniques.distinct: Forsythe's technologies are the most limb-led technique in the set (initiation 0.2): the limbs lead by drawing in space. Its closest neighbour, at 90%, is Nikolais/Louis, which also decentralises the body and analyses space, followed by Countertechnique and Gaga.

notes.grounding: Built on a ballet body: lifted, with quick footwork.
notes.torso: Off-centre torsos, tilts and twists arise as the body follows lines.
notes.dynamics: Can be very fast and articulated, often with sudden shifts.
notes.initiation: Imagined points and lines around the body lead the movement.
notes.structure: Clear rules, but the movement itself is improvised.
notes.fall: Off-balance, off-centre shapes are common; Forsythe pushes ballet off its axis.

techniques.why: Movement starts from imagined points and lines around the body, then is improvised with clear operations.

people.name: William Forsythe
people.path: Danced with the Joffrey Ballet and then the Stuttgart Ballet from 1973.
people.story: Forsythe directed Ballett Frankfurt (1984–2004) and The Forsythe Company (2005–2015). He took ballet's geometry apart, developed Improvisation Technologies with his dancers, and also made installations he called choreographic objects.
people.belief: Ballet is a living language whose rules can be analysed, broken and reassembled.

class.name: Point–point–line
class.desc: Drawing lines between points of the body and in space.
class.notice: The line is imagined; the body follows it.

class.name: Inscription and extrusion
class.desc: Drawing shapes with any body part and pushing them out into space.
class.notice: The elbow or knee can draw as well as the hand.

class.name: Dropping curves
class.desc: Letting curves fall through the body.
class.notice: The body yields where the curve passes.

class.name: Combining operations
class.desc: Several operations at once, improvised at speed.
class.notice: Many centres at the same time.

techniques.name: Flying Low
techniques.summary: A technique for moving quickly in and out of the floor in spirals, organised around the relationship between centre and periphery.
techniques.history: The Venezuelan dancer and teacher David Zambrano developed Flying Low in the 1990s while working mainly in Europe. He drew on release work, Contact Improvisation and his background in social dance. The technique trains dancers to travel efficiently close to the ground, using breath and spiralling paths so that going down and coming up flow continuously. Zambrano also created Passing Through, an improvisation method about moving through a group. Both are widely taught in European contemporary dance schools and festivals.
principles: Spiralling in and out of the floor
Moving fast close to the ground

concepts.desc: Keeping a clear relation between the body's centre and its extremities, especially at speed.
Paths that carry the body down to and up from the floor without stopping.
Exhaling to go down, using breath to drive speed and release.
Zambrano's related group improvisation practice of moving through and with others.

exercises: Low spirals in and out of the floor
Travelling sequences across the room at low level
Hands and feet supporting quick transfers
Group pathways moving through space together
works: Taught mainly as a practice rather than through repertoire
techniques.legacy: Common in European contemporary training; known for athletic, low-level speed.
techniques.distinct: Flying Low has the highest floor score (0.9) and is among the most grounded. Unlike Release and Butoh, which also go low, it is fast and dynamic. That combination of very low and very fast is what defines it.

notes.grounding: Weight is very low, with deep knees and a low centre.
notes.torso: Spirals drive the paths to and from the floor.
notes.dynamics: Fast, energetic and athletic, with quick shifts.
notes.floor: The defining feature: constant passage through low levels.
notes.initiation: Organised from the centre and breath.
notes.structure: Set sequences and principles mixed with improvisation.
notes.fall: The body constantly drops and recovers through the floor.
notes.contact: Group awareness and some partner work, but not shared weight.

techniques.why: Very low, very fast travel in and out of the floor, organised from the centre in spirals.

people.name: David Zambrano
people.path: Trained in Venezuela and New York, drawing on release, Contact Improvisation and social dance.
people.story: Based in Europe from the 1990s, Zambrano developed Flying Low and the group improvisation practice Passing Through, teaching worldwide.
people.belief: Move efficiently through the floor and through the group, connecting centre and periphery.

class.name: Breath and low stance
class.desc: Finding the low, wide stance with breath.
class.notice: Exhale to go down.

class.name: Spirals into the floor
class.desc: Spiralling down to the floor and through it.
class.notice: No stopping on the way down.

class.name: Up and travelling
class.desc: Pushing up from the floor and travelling low and fast.
class.notice: The centre stays low while the body travels.

techniques.name: Gaga
techniques.summary: A movement language taught through spoken images, focused on sensation, effort and pleasure, practised without mirrors.
techniques.history: Ohad Naharin danced with the Martha Graham Dance Company before founding his own and becoming artistic director of Batsheva Dance Company in Tel Aviv in 1990. He developed Gaga over the following years, first as training for Batsheva dancers. It later opened to the public as Gaga/people, with classes for non-dancers alongside Gaga/dancers. A teacher speaks images and instructions while everyone moves at once. There are no mirrors and no demonstrations to copy. The 2015 documentary Mr. Gaga brought it to a wide audience.

concepts.desc: A sense of the body being carried, with minimal effort, often the base layer of class.
Fast, small vibrations through the body that release tension and wake up sensation.
Adding instructions one on top of another, so the body carries many tasks at once.
Sudden bursts of speed and force that come out of softness rather than tension.

exercises: Continuous movement for the whole class, never stopping
Layering images: textures, speeds, body parts
Exploring extremes of effort, from minimal to explosive
techniques.legacy: Taught internationally to dancers and the public; reshaped Batsheva's style.
techniques.distinct: Gaga comes from a Graham dancer, yet it lands closer to Nikolais/Louis, Wigman and Forsythe than to Graham. It keeps Graham's mobile spine but drops the codified structure and the pelvic origin. Its strongest numbers are a very articulate torso (0.85) with low structure (0.2).

notes.grounding: Neither lifted nor sunk; the stance changes with the image.
notes.torso: A very fluid spine: undulating, shaking, curving.
notes.dynamics: A wide range, from floating to explosive.
notes.floor: Mostly standing; floor work is occasional.
notes.initiation: Sensation can start anywhere; often centre and spine.
notes.structure: Spoken images and tasks; no fixed steps.
notes.fall: Some off-balance play, but not a focus.
notes.contact: Dancers move together in a room but rarely touch.

techniques.why: Improvised from spoken images, with a very fluid, articulate spine and a wide dynamic range.

people.name: Ohad Naharin
people.path: Trained with Batsheva Dance Company, then in New York with Martha Graham's company, at Juilliard and the School of American Ballet.
people.story: Naharin became artistic director of Batsheva in 1990 and developed Gaga as its daily training, later opening it to the public. His works include Minus 16 and Decadance; the documentary Mr. Gaga (2015) traced his life.
people.belief: Listen to the body before telling it what to do; connect to pleasure and effort at the same time.

class.name: Float
class.desc: Floating: feeling the body carried with minimal effort.
class.notice: Constant, soft movement; no stopping.

class.name: Quake and textures
class.desc: Shaking and other textures layered on top.
class.notice: Small, fast vibrations through the whole body.

class.name: Spine waves
class.desc: Waves through the spine.
class.notice: The spine as a fluid chain.

class.name: Explosive and melt
class.desc: Sudden explosive reaches, then melting.
class.notice: Power comes out of softness.

techniques.name: Countertechnique
techniques.summary: A structured class and set of tools that use counter-directions to let dancers move big and off balance with less strain.
techniques.history: The Dutch choreographer Anouk van Dijk developed Countertechnique from the 1990s with her company in Amsterdam, and formalised it as a teachable system in the 2000s. She later directed Chunky Move in Melbourne. The technique responds to the demands of contemporary choreography: big, fast, off-balance movement. It aims to make that movement possible without overworking the body. Dancers learn to send body parts in opposite directions so that the body stays spacious and supported while it moves to extremes.
principles: Sending body parts in opposite directions
A dancer who thinks while moving

concepts.desc: For every direction one part moves in, another part goes the opposite way.
Briefly checking through the body during movement to release unnecessary tension.
Using counter-directions to stay supported in extreme positions.
Principles the dancer applies to any choreography, rather than a style of its own.

exercises: Combinations that test the tools at speed
techniques.legacy: Used as a training method in many European and Australian schools.
techniques.distinct: Countertechnique is the technique closest to the average of all eighteen. Its nearest neighbours are Taylor, Humphrey–Weidman and Nikolais/Louis. It has a structured class, a willingness to go off balance like the Humphrey–Limón line, and release roots.

notes.grounding: Balanced between lift and drop; counter-directions keep the body spacious.
notes.torso: Mobile, but organised by opposing directions rather than curving for its own sake.
notes.dynamics: Wide range, depending on the phrase.
notes.floor: Some floor work, but mostly standing and travelling.
notes.initiation: Directions are sent out from the centre and in from the periphery.
notes.structure: A structured class with tools rather than fixed shapes.
notes.fall: Designed to make big off-balance movement safe.

techniques.why: A set class with clear tools that uses counter-directions to go off balance safely.

people.name: Anouk van Dijk
people.path: Trained and danced in the Netherlands before founding her own company in Amsterdam.
people.story: Van Dijk developed Countertechnique from the 1990s to meet the demands of her own fast, off-balance choreography, and later directed Chunky Move in Melbourne.
people.belief: Moving big and fast doesn't have to mean strain: counter-directions create space and ease.

class.name: Scanning
class.desc: Scanning the body to release unnecessary tension.
class.notice: Less effort, more space.

class.name: Counter-directions
class.desc: Sending body parts in opposite directions.
class.notice: For every direction, an opposite one.

class.name: Big off-balance
class.desc: Large off-balance phrases at speed.
class.notice: Going far off balance without strain.
